query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers, the evolution of chemical short‐range order (SRO) at the nanometer‐scale interfaces governs the progressive plastic (creep) deformation under sustained loading by modifying local dislocation nucleation and mobility.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FCC/BCC HEA multilayers with a nanoscale coating structure having a relatively random or low-SRO state at the interfaces.
generation.intervention: A selective post-deposition annealing treatment designed to systematically enhance or modify the degree of short-range order within individual FCC and BCC layers while preserving the multilayer architecture.
generation.conditions: Sustained loading (creep conditions) at intermediate to elevated temperatures that promote dislocation motion, where the applied stress and temperature are kept constant between compared samples.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoscale interfaces between FCC and BCC layers, where the degree of chemical SRO can be varied by annealing and which in turn modulate dislocation-interface interactions.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced SRO at the interfaces is predicted to alter the local energy landscape for dislocation nucleation and mobility. If high SRO serves as an effective barrier or alters dislocation climb processes, it will change the creep rate by either retarding or modifying dislocation interactions compared with a baseline low-SRO state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Multilayers exhibiting a higher SRO contrast at the interfaces (achieved via controlled annealing) will show a measurable difference in creep response compared to unannealed samples – for example, a change in creep rate and/or dislocation density/distribution. Specifically, if SRO acts as an effective barrier, one might observe a reduced creep rate and different activation energy for plastic deformation relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: As-deposited HEA multilayers with minimal interfacial SRO, having a creep response governed by conventional dislocation climb mechanisms.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to samples that maintain a stable nanoscale multilayer structure and comparable overall composition; if the annealing parameters change the multilayer architecture (e.g., induce layer coarsening or phase separation beyond controlled SRO evolution), the mechanism may not be isolated.
generation.uncertainty: It is currently uncertain if the SRO evolution effect is dominant over other factors such as inherent lattice distortion or compositional gradients. The magnitude of the change in creep rate due solely to SRO variations is also not precisely known.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical FCC/BCC HEA multilayer samples. Subject one set to a post-deposition annealing treatment optimized to induce a high degree of interfacial SRO, while keeping the other set in its as-deposited, low-SRO state. Then, perform tensile creep tests at identical stress and temperature conditions on both sets while simultaneously characterizing the dislocation structures and interfacial features (using TEM, atom probe tomography, or similar techniques).
measurements: Creep rate (strain vs. time under constant load)
Activation energy and stress exponent from creep curves
Dislocation density and distribution at and near the interfaces
Degree of short-range order at the interfaces (using diffraction or spectroscopy methods)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the systematic variation of SRO (verified via microstructural characterization) does not result in any statistically significant differences in the creep rate, activation energy, or dislocation-interface interactions compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis that interfacial SRO evolution governs progressive plastic deformation can be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The tensile creep behavior of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy was systematically investigated over an intermediate temperature range (500–600 °C) and applied stress (140–400 MPa). The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II). The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol −1 , whereas the HSR showed much higher corresponding values of 8.9–14 and 380 kJ mol −1 . Microstructural examinations on the deformed samples revealed remarkable dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels. Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively. Moreover, dynamic precipitates identified as M 23 C 6 or a Cr-rich σ phase were formed along grain boundaries in HSR. The diffusion-compensated strain rate versus modulus-compensated stress data analysis implied that the creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

decision.trend: Early studies on HEAs under sustained loading – such as the tensile creep experiments in equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn (PMC7512559) – applied frameworks drawn from conventional metallic multilayers, where the deformation was largely interpreted in terms of stress‐assisted dislocation climb and dynamic recrystallization. However, these studies also hinted that the unique features of HEAs—namely severe lattice distortions and significant short-range order (SRO) effects—alter dislocation behavior. In conventional multilayers, the interface acts as a barrier or source for dislocations, but in FCC/BCC HEA multilayers the variation in chemistry and lattice distortion between layers suggests that the interface itself may modulate local SRO and dislocation mobility. Thus, early work tried to correlate creep rate with applied stress and temperature via bulk mechanisms but remained unsatisfied in isolating the contributions of SRO evolution versus lattice distortion at the nanoscale interfaces.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved whether the progressive plastic (creep) deformation in FCC/BCC HEA multilayers is controlled primarily by evolving chemical short‐range order at the layer interfaces (which could modify local dislocation nucleation and mobility) or by the gradients in lattice distortion inherent to the compositional complexity. A controlled comparison that directly varies the SRO state between layers while keeping the multilayer architecture constant is still lacking.
decision.lever: Selective post-deposition annealing treatment to systematically vary the degree of short-range order in the individual FCC and BCC layers
decision.why: This approach builds on the trend where conventional creep mechanisms were insufficient to fully capture HEA behavior. By tuning annealing temperature and duration, one can control the SRO development independently in each layer. Comparing creep responses for multilayers with different SRO contrasts – while preserving the nanoscale multilayer structure and overall composition – would directly test whether interfacial SRO variations govern dislocation dynamics and hence progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading. A finding that a stronger SRO contrast correlates with altered dislocation density, dislocation-interface interactions, and a measurable change in creep rate would support the hypothesis, whereas no change would falsify it.
